title: Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
description: , Mohammed Ghobari and Timour Azhari DUBAI/ADEN/RIYADH, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revo...
fullText:
DUBAI/ADEN/RIYADH, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.

Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi ​Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.

Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.

While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".

Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said.

A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had ‌held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the ⁠move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added.

Inside Yemen, five military sources from the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government said the Revolutionary Guards had directed ⁠the new Houthi campaign along the Red Sea coast, a flat, narrow plain known as the Tihama, starting with a blitz of rocket fire.

Citing communications intercepts and the accounts of captured Houthi prisoners, the Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being directed by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a top Revolutionary Guards commander.

Iranian sources were not immediately able to confirm that, though they had previously described Shahlaei, who is ​in ​the Guards' specialist Qods Force unit, as having spent time in Yemen in recent years.

The Guards were still ​able to move weapons and personnel in and out of Yemen despite ‌an aerial and maritime blockade of Houthi areas, the Iranian sources said without elaborating on how they did so.

"If we look at their offensive on the west coast, it's not something prepared just last week or last month," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group, describing the seizure of Mocha as a significant milestone in the war.

"The evolution of the Houthis was basically because of the new weapons they gained, either through the Iranians directly or through the different smuggling networks that they are counting on," Nagi said, pointing specifically at their use of drones in the latest offensive.

As the Houthis began an advance towards Mocha last week, Yemen's government requested more air support and other help from the Saudis, two more Yemeni officials said.

It ‌was seeking a Saudi air campaign against Houthi targets in the Houthi heartland including Sanaa and key strategic ​assets such as oil depots, they said.

However, the kingdom stuck to providing logistical, armament and intelligence support with only ​limited air strikes that were focused on northern battlefronts in Jawf and Marib provinces, ​areas the government regarded as less important.

The officials' own assessment was that Riyadh was anxious to avoid a major escalation with the Houthis for fear ‌of provoking heavier drone strikes on Saudi territory.

Saudi officials did not immediately ​respond to Reuters requests for comment on Riyadh's ​military focus on the northern front rather than the Red Sea coast and other big Houthi targets.

The overall military situation in Yemen is hard to gauge after a years-long pause in major warfare since a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia have invested in forces they back there. But the pro-government coalition has suffered ​from internal splits.

Although previous rounds of warfare in the Tihama had produced ‌sudden advances and retreats, it remains unclear if Saudi-backed forces can easily dislodge the Houthis this time, Nagi said.

"Maybe we can see some advances from the government ​if they get the necessary support from the Saudis. But that could be a bit difficult this time," he said.

title: Coroner shares details on 2 infant deaths amid Pennsylvania measles outbreak
description: A Pennsylvania coroner confirmed the state's two measles-related deaths last month both involved infants, and the virus itself caused one of them.
fullText:
A Pennsylvania coroner confirmed Wednesday that the state's two measles-related deaths last month both involved infants, and that the virus caused one of the deaths.

Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, Lancaster County's coroner, said Ivan Miller died Aug. 14 shortly after his birth of a ruptured spleen, and 6-week-old Mary Stoltzfus died Aug. 18 at her home from a measles infection, according to the Associated Press and The Washington Post.

A genetic birth defect called Amish lethal microcephaly, which causes a small head and underdeveloped brain, left Stoltzfus highly vulnerable to an infection, he explained to the outlets.

Diamantoni said he released the information in response to a state right-to-know law request by WPMT-TV, Fox 43.

USA TODAY reached out to the coroner's office for comment.

Diamantoni's office didn't perform an autopsy on Stoltzfus, so the cause of death was determined by her doctors, he told the AP.

Diamantoni's office did autopsy Miller, and determined that he died of a ruptured spleen. While Miller was infected with measles − which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor − Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that the virus is noted only because it was considered "a significant condition" at the time of death.

Neither was old enough to be vaccinated, as the first dose is typically given around age 1.

These deaths have come under national scrutiny and political debate.

Last month, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked for the two deaths reported by Pennsylvania's health department to be removed from the CDC's national tally of measles cases, questioning whether the virus was the cause. CDC staffers had already accepted the state's characterization of the deaths as linked to measles before Kennedy's request.

Last week, Kennedy acknowledged that measles caused the recent death of one Pennsylvania infant, citing information from the county coroner, but suggested that the federal government would not yet recognize the fatality in official data amid a fast-growing national outbreak.

Public health experts said the move amounted to extraordinary political interference in the authority of a state health department and an effort to minimize the risks of the highly infectious virus.

U.S. measles cases have hit their highest level in more than three decades under President Donald Trump and Kennedy, his top health official and a long-time vaccine skeptic. Kennedy has promoted the idea that vaccines, including the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot, are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, despite decades of scientific evidence that the shots save lives.

Leading medical organizations say that Kennedy's statements about vaccines and his policies as health secretary, including efforts to reduce the number of government-recommended childhood immunizations, have increased vaccine hesitancy, making outbreaks harder to curb.

title: Africa's top health body warns Congo’s Ebola outbreak is rapidly spreading beyond epicenter
description: The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record in eastern Congo is rapidly spreading beyond its epicenter, Africa’s top health body said Thursday.  In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in...
fullText:
KINSHASA, Congo (AP) — The fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record in eastern Congo is rapidly spreading beyond its epicenter, Africa's top health body said Thursday.

In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak's epicenter, but risen sharply in neighboring North Kivu and Haut-Uele, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said at a weekly briefing.

According to the latest government figures released on Thursday, 6,843 cases have been reported, including 3,310 deaths. Ituri province remains the hardest-hit province, with more than 5,400 cases while North Kivu has reported over 1,000 cases since the outbreak was declared in May.

The outbreak in eastern Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

In North Kivu, new cases more than doubled to 381 in the latest three-week period, from 165 in the earlier period, Yap Boum, Africa CDC's head of emergency preparedness and response, said Thursday.

The virus recently reached two more health zones in North Kivu, where fighting between government forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels, who control the provincial capital Goma, has complicated the response.

Last month, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type called Zaire.

Clinical trials are underway to find a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus.

The vaccination trials started in the eastern Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele provinces, Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said Thursday.

Kingebeni said the vaccination campaign initially targeted newly affected provinces to help prevent further spread. Vaccinations in Ituri are set to start next week, he added.

A key challenge is the limited supply of doses, said Kingebeni. Congo has received 70,000 doses so far.

Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal.

title: It’s not just food: The plastic packaging your food comes in may carry cancer-linked chemicals, and most go untested
description: The government is replacing harmful chemicals in your food packaging—but they may be unknowingly making it worse.
fullText:
It looks like the American consumer has more to worry about than food recalls and cyclospora—a new study found that even the packaging the food comes in may pose some health concerns.

Out of over 15,000 food contact chemicals (FCCs), 1,222 or 8% can pose serious health risks, according to a recent study published in the peer-reviewed journal Environmental Science & Technology. Some of these FCCs, which in general are "substances that come into contact with food, such as through food packaging, processing, storage or other handling," per the FDA, were found to be hazardous to human health.

Researchers from the nonprofit Food Packaging Forum Foundation, which conducted the study, found at least 2,160 chemicals regularly contact food and "migrate into foodstuffs." Using guidelines from the UN's Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals (GHS), researchers found some of the chemicals related to food packaging and other materials were "carcinogenic, mutagenic, toxic to reproduction, harmful to specific organs after repeated exposure, [and] endocrine disrupting."

That's not the only concerning part. The researchers found that 13,211 of the 15,159 known food-contact chemicals lacked harmonized hazard data. That means the scientists could not determine from the available data whether those chemicals met the study's criteria for being hazardous.

"There's a lot of ways of establishing whether something is hazardous or not, and some methods are based very much just on computer models, looking at the structure, predicting something. And others are based on in vitro tests," Dr. Helene Wiesinger, scientific communication officer at the nonprofit and one of the researchers on the study, told Fortune. "And in some sense, the data that we used?' So this is the data we used, and the problem we ran into at that point was that there were huge data lags."

Those "data lags" have proved to be an ongoing issue throughout the food safety process. She said that it creates a problem regulators have faced across the chemicals industry—removing a known hazardous substance doesn't necessarily solve the problem if it's replaced with a structurally similar chemical that has also never been adequately tested.

A large majority of the chemicals that contact food regularly are under-researched and lack the necessary information to estimate their risks, Wiesinger said. She said researchers refer to this as "regrettable substitution," where a governing body may unknowingly expose consumers to other dangerous chemicals by removing a known one.

"So take bisphenol A, and we say we don't want to use bisphenol A anymore, so we use bisphenol S instead, because it's functionally similar," Wiesinger said, referring to two chemicals used in plastics and thermal receipts. "It has, in a sense, similar ways it can be used in the industry—so it's an easy substitute. But it didn't have enough data," she said, to "the point where the replacement was searched for, and then bisphenol S was used, and then later, it turned out to be similarly problematic as bisphenol A."

Bisphenol A is a common chemical found primarily in water bottles and other various products—and according to the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, roughly 93% of people over the age of six have detectable levels of the chemical. Bisphenol S is a common replacement for Bisephenol A—but it has been found to cause negative hormonal effects "comparable to or worse" than its predecessor, based on a study from the National Library of Medicine.

The study attempted to address that problem by looking beyond the individual chemicals. Wiesinger grouped the 15,159 FCCs according to chemical structures and identified specific "priority groups," or clusters of chemicals structurally similar to ones already known to be hazardous. Among those groups were ortho-phthalates and known "forever chemicals" like PFASs. According to the FDA's recall website, there have been no open recalls regarding food packaging.

About 70% of the over 4,000 chemicals fell into the priority groups, essentially meaning a hazardous chemical could potentially fly under the radar not because scientists have established that it is safe, but because scientists don't have enough information to determine if it's dangerous.

But Wiesinger warned that even if the conclusions of the study may be concerning for food consumers, the findings are most effective in the hands of policymakers. She said it would be "a bit of a policy failure" if a hazardous material can simply be replaced with another that hasn't been adequately tested, and that comes with testing materials worldwide.

"Our data base is global," Wiesinger said. "There is a lot of trade from all places to all places that we have data for."

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: OpenAI pulls out of Caltech math hackathon after mathematicians issue open letter criticizing AI math 'slop'
description: Caltech mathematicians said the event, which is sponsored by AI companies, "is likely to have destructive impacts for the mathematical community."
fullText:
OpenAI pulled its sponsorship of Caltech's AI math hackathon.

Mathematicians warned the event could fuel "slop mathematics."

Event organizers said they intended for the event to be a showcase for responsible AI use.

The latest math problem OpenAI is trying to solve is a bunch of angry mathematicians.

A researcher at OpenAI said on Thursday that the ChatGPT maker is no longer sponsoring Caltech's "math hackathon," an event where participants use large language models to solve research problems.

OpenAI's exit follows an open letter released on Wednesday from current and former Caltech mathematicians, who said the event, which is sponsored by AI companies, "is likely to have destructive impacts for the mathematical community."

"We recognize that the rapid progress of AI in mathematics is disruptive," Dan Roberts, OpenAI's research lead, said on X. "We're looking to engage with the math community more on the best way to integrate this technology and communicate its impacts."

At issue, according to the mathematicians, is the manner in which AI companies claim to solve outstanding theoretical problems using their models and then leave practical applications and proofs to actual researchers. They call this "slop mathematics."

"After the latest result is dropped, research mathematicians are compelled to step in to properly verify, disseminate, and sometimes discredit entirely the claimed results," the academics said. "This labor goes uncompensated, uncredited, and unacknowledged."

The drama reached a fever pitch on Tuesday when OpenAI announced its agents had solved the Navier-Stokes equations, a 90-year-old set of mathematical formulas that can predict how liquids and gases move.

Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematician who, alongside another academic, published research on the problem on Monday, said on Tuesday that OpenAI might have used his conversations with AI chatbots, including OpenAI's, to arrive at a solution. OpenAI said it couldn't rule out that "de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠."

The mathematicians also said they believed the CalTech event would serve as unfair advertising for AI companies, who "will take credit for the effort of talented undergrads."

Anthropic, which is also sponsoring the event, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. Nor did OpenAI.

The "mathathon" is billed as a practice ground for young mathematicians to "responsibly use AI tools to augment human understanding of mathematics," according to an application page.

Event organizers, many of whom are undergraduates, said in a response letter on Thursday that they didn't intend to cause such a stir.

"Events like Mathathon encourage young people to stay excited about mathematics, engage their interests with modern tools, and maintain hope in a confusing time," the organizers wrote. "It's our first time running an event at this scale, and we are grateful for all the feedback we have received."

As designed, participants in the mathathon will compete in a first round, where they're given 40 hours and $20,000 in tokens to solve an open problem.

Then, a certain number of teams whose answers are "promising and well explained" will advance to the second round, where they receive six months and additional AI tokens to further their work.

Anthropic and OpenAI agreed to support the event by donating $2 million in AI credits. It was unclear on Thursday how many of those tokens were provided by OpenAI, and what happens to them now.

title: Scott Bessent dared the $32 trillion bond market with ‘I am the house now’ statement. It didn’t listen
description: After helping lift the yen, Bessent is finding the much larger Treasury market harder to tame as yields push toward 5%.
fullText:
Speaking at Southern Methodist University on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dared currency traders, and indirectly the bond market, to challenge him as he wages a multi-front battle to stabilize markets amid Iran war turmoil while also trying to slow rising yields that threaten to make government borrowing more costly.

"I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do," Bessent said. "And you can bet against me if you want."

In late July, the U.S. joined Japanese officials in buying yen in order to prop up the struggling currency. Although it wasn't the Treasury's stated intention, one concern surrounding its intervention was the risk that Japan, one of the largest holders of U.S. government debt, would offload a large chunk of U.S. treasuries to right the ship, which could send U.S. Treasury yields higher. Yields rise as the price of bonds fall.

Following the joint intervention, the yen has strengthened against the dollar, and this week it surged to a nearly seven-month high in Asia, showing stability likely celebrated by Bessent, who had previously said the yen was "undervalued."

In the $32 trillion Treasury market—simply the world's most important, as it funds the U.S. government, sets global borrowing costs, and serves as the ultimate safe haven—Bessent's warnings and actions have so far gone unheeded.

The Treasury Department said Wednesday it would buy a maximum of $6 billion of 10- to 20-year bonds—above the $4 billion minimum it said it would buy last month. The buybacks are officially intended to add liquidity to the market, the Treasury Department said, but they also could help push yields down by adding demand. Yields are going up, though.

On Thursday, yields for 10-, 20- and 30-year Treasuries surged. The yield on the 10-year, which serves as a benchmark, hit 4.93% Thursday, its highest level since 2023 and dangerously close to exceeding 5%—a level it has only reached once before in the last two decades.

"Normally, when these red lines are put out, people like to test them," Thomas Kikis, the head of markets for the U.S. & Americas at British bank Standard Chartered, told Fortune. "The market's gonna give him a bit of a run over the next few days."

White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement to Fortune that Bessent's past history of intervention with the Argentine peso last year shows just how effective Bessent can be at stabilizing markets.

title: Judge accused of enabling immigrant to escape ICE gets a rare public reprimand
description: The highest court in Massachusetts on Thursday issued a public reprimand against a district court judge who was accused of allowing an immigrant to escape U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement cust...
fullText:
BOSTON (AP) — The highest court in Massachusetts on Thursday issued a public reprimand against a district court judge who was accused of allowing an immigrant to escape U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

The case dates back to 2018 when Judge Shelley Joseph was accused of colluding with the immigrant's attorney and a court officer to allow him to escape out a back door of the courthouse after a hearing on charges that included drug possession.

The decision by the Supreme Judicial Court follows a recommendation for the reprimand by a hearing officer for the Commission on Judicial Conduct. It concluded that Joseph created the appearance of impropriety and failed to comply with the law.

"The respondent's statements during that conversation, including her proposal to detain (the immigrant) overnight in State custody, and her conduct in instructing the clerk to turn off the court room audio recording system, created an appearance of impropriety in violation of her duties," according to the Supreme Judicial Court ruling.

Joseph's attorney, Elizabeth Mulvey, argued at the commission hearing last year that the case had been distorted over time and that everyone had come to believe that her client "let an illegal immigrant out of the door" with half the public believing she should be jailed and the other half calling her a "folk hero."

Mulvey also argued that Joseph had been vilified in the media and people were giving the impression that "dozens of people" had seen Joseph "get off the bench, escort the defendant to the door, give him a hug and wish him Godspeed."

On Thursday, Mulvey acknowledged that it had been an "incredibly long and difficult eight years for Judge Joseph."

"We are grateful to the hearing officer who undertook this monumental task and pleased that his efforts have shown that this was a baseless federal prosecution from the beginning and solely the work of the defense lawyer involved," Mulvey said in a statement. "Judge Joseph is thankful for everyone who stood by her and looks forward to rejoining her colleagues."

The case is similar to that of a former Wisconsin judge who was convicted in December of felony obstruction for helping a man evade immigration authorities. The case has escalated a clash between the Trump administration and local authorities over the Republican president's sweeping immigration crackdown.

Last year, Hannah Dugan escorted a man and his lawyer out of her courtroom through the jury door after learning that immigration authorities were seeking his arrest. The man was taken into custody outside the courthouse after agents chased him on foot.

Dugan resigned the Milwaukee County circuit judgeship she had held for nine years in January amid threats of impeachment from Republican state lawmakers who labeled her an activist judge. In her resignation letter, she said her prosecution threatened "the independence of our judiciary." Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a fierce Trump loyalist running for Wisconsin governor, had urged authorities to "lock her up."

Then in July, U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman fined Dugan $5,000, describing the case as a situation where an otherwise good person, upset by immigration policies in this country, made a bad decision in the moment. She was spared prison time.

In the Massachusetts case, Joseph and a court officer were charged in 2019 with obstruction of justice. Those charges against Joseph were dropped in 2022 after she agreed to refer herself to a state agency that investigates allegations of misconduct by members of the bench.

That agency, the Commission on Judicial Conduct, concluded that Joseph "engaged in willful judicial misconduct that brought the judicial office into disrepute, as well as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice and unbecoming a judicial officer."

After her federal indictment in April 2019, Joseph was suspended from judicial duties and unable to work for over three years. Joseph, who remains a judge, was assigned in December to administrative duties in the Boston Municipal Court, and that is where she will resume her judicial responsibilities.

fullText:
A new poll shows the Texas governor's race has swung to a dead heat — erasing the lead Gov. Greg Abbott had held over his Democratic challenger for months.

The N+ Univision Sept. 9 poll showed the Republican incumbent and Democrat Gina Hinojosa tied at 47%, with 5% undecided, and was released the day Republicans convened in Texas for their first midterm convention.

The poll also showed that Democrat state Rep. James Talarico has a narrow edge over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 48% to 43%, with 7% undecided in the Texas Senate race.

Here's a deeper dive into the poll for the Texas governor's race and where the race stands.

The poll was conducted from Aug. 27 to Sept. 4 and surveyed 1,000 registered voters in Texas. Because the poll was not a probability sample, it has no traditional margin of error; instead, the equivalent margin of error for a matched, propensity-score sampling design is plus or minus 3.6 percentage points.

Overall, the N+ Univision poll showed that since the 2024 election, Texas voters have shifted 8 points more toward Democrats, with 25% saying they have become more supportive of Democrats and 17% saying they have become more supportive of Republicans.

Among Hispanic voters, the shift is even larger, at 11 points. The single most-cited reason for changing views was President Donald Trump's actions as president, named by 25% of voters in the poll and 24% of Hispanic voters.

The poll also found that 44% of voters view Abbott favorably and 47% unfavorably, while 42% view Hinojosa favorably and 29% unfavorably.

Abbott also has a negative favorability rating among Hispanic voters, sitting at 41% to 50%.

The N+ Univision Sept. 9 poll follows a Texas Public Opinion Research Aug. 27 poll that showed Abbott pulling further ahead of Hinojosa, 49% to 42% with 6% undecided.

Last month, the Cook Political Report on Aug. 20 moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" for several reasons.

But the report said it would adjust its findings as the race enters the final stretch to Election Day and once Abbott starts using attack ads to define Hinojosa — who the polls still show Texas voters are trying to get to know.

These two polls follow a summer of polls that showed the race between the two had been within the single digits:

Texas Pulse (Aug. 7): Abbott 46%, Hinojosa 45%.

Texas Southern University (Aug. 4): Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 43%.

title: India to push BRICS digital currency link despite hurdles, sources say
description: India is pushing to link central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) across BRICS nations for cross-border payments at a summit later this
fullText:
NEW DELHI, Sept 10 (Reuters) - India is pushing to link central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) across BRICS nations for cross-border payments at a summit later this week, ‌despite political and technical hurdles that could limit progress, two sources familiar with the discussions said.

India ‌is chairing BRICS this year, with leaders of the bloc set to meet in New Delhi on September 12 to 13. The ​Reserve Bank of India (RBI) proposed linking the countries' official digital currencies to facilitate cross-border trade, Reuters reported in January.

The BRICS grouping includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

The proposal to link CBDCs would be a part of the agenda for the leaders' meeting, the sources ‌said, although the limited adoption of ⁠digital currencies globally could complicate implementation. They did not want to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue and because they are not authorised to speak to ⁠media.

Emails sent to India's external affairs and federal finance ministries and the RBI were not answered.

POLITICAL, TECHNICAL CHALLENGES

India's proposal will build on the 2025 declaration at the BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, which pushed for interoperability between members' ​payment systems ​to make cross-border transactions more efficient.

Any move towards linking ​CBDCs, however, is likely to face significant challenges. ‌Previous discussions within BRICS on creating shared payment mechanisms have made little headway, underscoring the difficulties of integrating financial infrastructure across a diverse group of countries.

Strained relations between countries, such as Iran and the UAE, will remain a sticking point, with the UAE having cut financial ties with Iran, one of the two sources said.

India has also been reluctant to deepen financial connectivity with China, the second source said, adding that such arrangements ‌would require deeper trust between the neighbours. India stalled Alipay+'s ​proposal to link with the country's instant payments system for cross-border ​transactions over national security concerns due to its ​Chinese links, Reuters reported.

Currency-swap arrangements would also be needed to help manage trade imbalances ‌before any CBDC linkage could become operational, the ​source added.

BRICS nations have previously ​explored alternatives to dollar-based payments, including a proposal by Brazil for a common currency for the group, though the plan never advanced. U.S. President Donald Trump had warned the bloc against such a ​move by threatening to impose high ‌tariffs.

India has no interest in replacing the dollar, and linking official digital currencies is aimed at making ​cross-border payments easier and faster, the second source said.

title: Buc-ee's continues to protect its beaver logo. It just won $850K
description: Buc-ee's won more than $850,000 in a trademark lawsuit after a South Carolina retailer used a logo resembling its famous beaver.
fullText:
Buc-ee's has won another legal battle to protect its famous beaver mascot.

A federal judge has ordered South Carolina clothing retailer Born United to pay more than $850,000 after the company admitted to infringing on Buc-ee's trademark, according to the Greenville News, part of the USA TODAY Network. The judgment permanently prohibits Born United from using Buc-ee's beaver logo or any mark considered "confusingly similar."

The order also requires Born United to destroy merchandise bearing the disputed logo, remove advertisements featuring it and could require the company to pay Buc-ee's attorney fees if it violates the terms of the judgment.

The ruling is the latest victory for the Texas-based travel center chain, which has aggressively defended its trademarks as it expands across the United States. Buc-ee's has filed a number of lawsuits in recent years against businesses it says copied elements of its branding, including its recognizable smiling beaver mascot.

More news: Buc-ee's CEO eyes 'conservative, business-friendly states' for expansion

Buc-ee's filed the federal lawsuit against Born United in 2025, alleging the North Charleston retailer sold clothing featuring a version of the company's trademarked beaver logo.

According to Greenville News, some of the merchandise depicted a beaver resembling Buc-ee's mascot wearing tactical gear, including night-vision goggles and carrying a weapon. Buc-ee's argued the designs infringed on its federally registered trademarks and could lead customers to believe the products were affiliated with the company.

Born United agreed to settle the case by paying approximately $850,000 and permanently stopping use of Buc-ee's beaver logo or similar designs. The judgment also requires the company to destroy remaining products bearing the disputed logo and remove advertisements featuring the image.

Born United is a South Carolina clothing company with stores in North Charleston, Myrtle Beach and Summerville.

The retailer sells military-themed apparel and accessories through several brands. On its website, Born United says it "respects, supports and honors" members of the military, law enforcement, firefighters, first responders and others who serve the country.

The Born United case is one of several trademark disputes Buc-ee's has pursued as the company continues expanding beyond its Texas roots.

Most recently, Buc-ee's sued Beaver's Mini Mart, a family-owned convenience store in Beavercreek, Ohio. According to the federal complaint, Buc-ee's alleges the store's smiling beaver logo, name and red-letter branding are similar enough to its trademarks to create consumer confusion. The Ohio business has denied intentionally copying Buc-ee's branding.

fullText:
Apple recently announced some big changes to the Health app, as well as new sensors in the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. The company bundled these and other health-related announcements together, but that doesn't mean you need an Apple Watch 12 to take advantage of all the new features. Here's the breakdown of which Apple Watches will get the new features—and which ones don't need an Apple Watch at all.

You'll need the new Series 12 or the Ultra 4 to get Apple's new heart rate sensor—the one it's billing as the most accurate in any wearable. (Huge if true.) These two watches also have the new S11 processing chip. The sensor and the chip are required for what Apple is calling its "health sensing system," which gives you more frequent heart rate and HRV readings throughout the day.

According to Apple, the new systems measure heart rate every five seconds instead of every five minutes, and HRV every five minutes instead of every few hours. Overnight vitals will now include a Recovery HRV score that's compared to your baseline (so you know when your body is under more or less stress than usual). The Readiness score seems to rely on these readings, so you'll need one of the new watches to get that score.

I recently wrote about the changes Apple has planned for the new Health app and noted that those are likely to be software changes that don't require a new phone or watch. Apple writes in a footnote on the Apple Watch page that the redesigned Health app requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (or iPad). The full list of Apple Intelligence-enabled devices is here, and they include the iPhone 15 Pro and all iPhones 16 and newer.

The new app includes "insights," which seem to be similar to the trends you'll see in the current Apple Health app. If you've ever noticed the little cards that say things like "your cardio fitness has been trending up for 8 weeks," it seems we'll get more of those, and they'll be collected together into their own area of the app. There will also be text summaries of your data and recommendations for what to do next, apparently written by Apple Intelligence based on your data.

The new Health app includes an on-demand VO2max test you can do indoors. Apple's event video showed a person propping up their phone on the floor, making sure the phone's camera could see their entire body, and then following along with a metronome by stepping in place on the beat. You'll need a heart rate sensor to do this test and get your results, and Apple says that any Apple Watch will do—or AirPods Pro 3, or a third-party sensor.

In other words, it sounds like it can work with any device that broadcasts heart rate, which includes just about any wearable out there. If you have a Fitbit, a Whoop, or a Garmin (to name a few), you can probably get it to broadcast your heart rate and thus work with this test. Apple's Fitness app can already read heart rate from these devices, so I expect the compatibility to be the same for the VO2max test.

Workout Buddy, which takes the form of a motivational voice in your ear during workouts, requires Apple Intelligence. Previously, this meant you needed to carry an Apple Intelligence-enabled phone with you during workouts, but that's changing. The new Workout Buddy can work from your Apple Watch without needing a phone, so long as your watch has access to the Internet through either cellular data or a wifi network (such as your gym's wifi). Compatible watches include the Series 9 and newer, the Ultra 2 and later, or the Apple Watch SE 3.

title: 10 Hacks Every Libby User Should Know
description: If you're a reader (or listener), you'll want to take advantage of these Libby hacks for borrowing, organizing, and maximizing your loans.
fullText:
Libby is a service that connects users to their local library systems, giving them access to an enormous catalog of digital content, including e-books, audiobooks, and magazines—for free. If you're a reader (or listener), you'll want to take advantage of these Libby tips and tricks for borrowing, organizing, and maximizing your loans.

You're not limited to one library system on Libby. The platform allows you to connect to multiple libraries, so you can take advantage of larger catalogs in case one library has more titles or a shorter wait times for books you want to read. You still have to be eligible for a library card at every library you connect to, but you could add your city library, your county library, and a school library to your account (or even take advantage of a friend's or family member's card from a different city). Go to Menu > Add Library and search by library name, city, or zip code. Select the library to browse its collection, and follow the prompts to add that library's card if you qualify.

Libby automatically returns titles as soon as your loans expire, so unlike with physical books, you can't take extra time to finish up. But if you're reading on a Kindle, you may be able to borrow the title and immediately set your device to airplane mode to freeze the loan. While your Kindle is offline, you can return the title via the Libby app so the next person can borrow it. Note that there are reports that this workaround, which is unique to Kindle, may no longer be available on newer devices running the latest software, but Reddit users suggest that changing the date on your Kindle to before the return deadline and/or keeping the expired book open could also help avoid this issue.

If you like to track your reading history, you can export a timeline of your activity, which can be saved in a personal spreadsheet or uploaded to Goodreads. Tap Shelf > Timeline > Actions > Export Timeline and choose a format—Table creates a shareable HTML page, while Spreadsheet downloads an editable sheet to your device (JSON is also an option). Exports include information like the title name, author, borrow date, publisher, and ISBN. If syncing to Goodreads, choose Spreadsheet and follow the platform's import instructions.

Libby's tag system makes it easy to organize and sort titles across multiple lists, such as annual reading lists, favorites, or TBR (to name a few). Simply go to Tags > Actions > New Tag, add a name and description, and tap Create. When you want to add a title to one of these lists, hit Save on the title's page and select all relevant tags. Tap Tags on the bottom navigation to sort or filter tagged titles.

Not all new releases are immediately available to every library system, but you can get a head start on borrowing with the "Notify Me" smart tag, which will alert you when your library adds titles you've tagged. When you find a title via search that your library doesn't offer, you'll be prompted to create a Notify Me tag. You can also manually create one by following the process for custom tags and selecting Notify Me to turn it into a smart tag. This tag also works for new magazine issues and new content from specific authors or book series. Make sure you have push notifications enabled for Libby.

If you finish one book and want to immediately start another, you can use a search filter to find titles that are available now rather than sorting through wait lists. Then, you can pin that filter so every search—even if other filters are applied—shows you only titles that are ready to borrow. Go to Search and tap the three horizontal lines to open the filter list. Select available now > Show Titles, then press and hold the filter to open the pop-up menu and tap Pin Filter. You can follow the same process with other filters (if you only want to see books and/or audiobooks, for example). Note that subject filters can't be pinned.

Audiobooks can be storage hogs, and if you're listening to more than one title at a time, you may not want to devote that much of your device's space to those files. Customize how titles are downloaded versus streamed via Menu > Settings > Download Rules, where you can choose whether to automatically download everything, nothing, or only titles under 20 MB as well as enable downloads on wifi only (to avoid mobile data usage).

If you like to highlight passages or add notes to books as you read, you can review these annotations for titles borrowed via Libby even after you've returned them. In the Libby app, find the title and tap the cover image, then tap Reading Journey. You can also export these data via Actions > Export Reading Data. If you read the title on a Kindle device, notes and highlights are also saved on Amazon and visible on Goodreads.

Popular titles and new releases often rack up hundreds of holds in a short amount of time, meaning you could be waiting months before a copy is available at your library. Some library systems will designate a few copies of these books as "skip the line," meaning that they can't be reserved or renewed and instead are claimed on a first-come-first-serve basis once returned by the previous user. These titles are marked with a shamrock icon, and if your library offers them, you can find them via Search > Catalog Filters > skip the line.

If you have a long list of holds with varying wait times, you may occasionally have one or more books ready to borrow around the same time. If you're not ready to read a title as soon as it becomes available, you can opt to suspend your hold until you're done with the book you're currently reading or have more time to start something new. This keeps your place in line, so the book will be yours as soon as you un-suspend your hold and the title is returned by the current user. In the app, go to Shelf > Holds > Manage Hold > Suspend Hold, or tap Suspend next to the title if it is ready to borrow.

title: Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia
description: Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.
fullText:
Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and that the Briton does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.

Garcia, 28, makes the first defence of his belt against Benn at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday.

The American has consistently dismissed Benn's ability during the build-up and, after skipping Tuesday's face-off, has been accused overlooking the 29-year-old.

But Garcia says he is not taking anything lightly as he aims for a 26th win in 29 bouts as a professional.

Asked whether Benn, who has not fought at welterweight since April 2022, deserves the opportunity to challenge for a world title, Garcia said: "Not at all."

He told BBC Sport: "He's an average fighter, he's athletic and it's his last name. It's not a shot at him; it's just the bitter truth.

"I'm preparing like he's the best fighter in the world. It's all about preparation and how sharp you are.

"People could say you're overlooking him. No, I'm calling it how I see it.

"Do you want me to say he's as good as Floyd Mayweather? He's not.

"He's alright. He comes forward and throws looping overhands. He's aggressive and will make him a rugged fight, but it's not something I haven't seen before."

Garcia and Benn have documented their fight camps on social media, but have presented their preparations in different ways.

Benn has posted videos of his training regime, while Garcia has been collaborating with influencers and making appearances in the WWE.

"He's not my cup of tea. I wouldn't want to hang out with him too much," Garcia said.

"He's a bit of a hypocrite and contradicts himself a lot. I am who I am - goofy and outgoing, making jokes and having fun.

"He is trying to say he's humble, but he's out here any chance in a Rolls Royce. He loves the lights.

"He thinks I'm like that, but I'm focused on my craft 100%."

title: Davies sinks world champion Wu at English Open

Welsh prospect Davies, 20, opened up a 3-0 lead on his way to the first ranking event quarter-final of his career, helped by a break of 105 in the second frame, then completed his victory as China's Wu struggled to find his dynamic best form.

Selby led 2-0 in the all-English tussle after an early break of 112 but then lost the next three frames. He dragged himself level, but Wilson trebled in the yellow to effectively make sure of victory in the decider.

title: Weight-loss drugs avoid Wada banned list for 2027
description: Athletes will not be banned from using weight-loss drugs, but the substances will remain on a monitoring list.
fullText:
Athletes will not be banned from taking weight-loss drugs under the World Anti-Doping Agency's rules for 2027, but the substances will remain on its monitoring list.

Wada confirmed the decision following a meeting of its executive committee as it continues to examine the potential of the drugs, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, to enhance performance and the risk of abuse in sport.

The rules take effect in January and are reviewed annually.

Medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro have become increasingly common outside elite sport.

The 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams revealed last year - while on a break from professional tennis - that she had been using weight-loss medication.

Professor Olivier Rabin, Wada's senior director for science and medicine, warned athletes to be "very careful using those drugs and never without medical advice and supervision".

"It's such a drastic change in your physiology that it can come with serious side effects and risks, in particular for athletes," he told BBC Sport.

Semaglutide, often marketed under the Ozempic and Wegovy banners, was first placed on Wada's monitoring list in 2024. Tirzepatide, commonly branded as Mounjaro, was added this year.

For a substance to move from the monitoring list to the prohibited list, it needs to meet two of three criteria: that it can enhance sport performance, it poses a health risk to an athlete, or it violates the spirit of sport.

Wada has started one study and is preparing another to examine the effects of the drugs in conditions designed to mimic high-level exercise.

"It's still going to take us a little bit of time to collect all this information, because they are highly controlled studies in very specific conditions," said Rabin.

"What we want to see is whether some of the pharmacological impact on human physiology that has been observed in obese patients would also occur in non-obese, highly trained people."

Rabin said potential benefits could also be offset by side effects such as nausea, fatigue and the loss of muscle mass.

"If you're an athlete and you lose muscle mass, that may be very counterproductive for what you're trying to achieve," he said.

"So all these elements show you that it's not a very straightforward answer."

Under the usual timetable, a change approved at next September's executive committee meeting would take effect in January 2028.

Weight-loss drugs seem most likely to appeal to athletes in weight-category sports such as boxing and wrestling, as well as horse racing, where jockeys have to meet strict weight requirements.

"A lot of sports would benefit from weight control and weight management," said Rabin.

"Not only those in weight-category sports, but all sorts of sports."

He highlighted long-distance runners and cyclists as other athletes with weight control "very high on their agenda".

"There are sports as well where aesthetics play a role," he said. "It can be gymnastics, can be horse riding, can be many different sports where you don't have weight categories, but physical appearance is quite important."

Very few athletes have spoken publicly about using weight-loss drugs. The most high-profile is Williams, who said she struggled to lose weight after having children.

She is also a spokesperson for Ro, a company which sells GLP-1s and in which her husband is an investor.

A recent Loughborough University study,, external which surveyed more than 100 sports medicine physicians around the world, found 12% were aware of athletes using GLP-1 drugs despite having no medical need for them.

title: Fenerbahce boss stuns club by quitting after Roma draw
description: Ismail Kartal resigns as Fenerbahce's head coach just minutes after the Turkish side's 1-1 draw with Roma in the Champions League.
fullText:
Ismail Kartal resigned as head coach of Fenerbahce just minutes after the Turkish side's 1-1 draw with Roma in the Champions League.

Kartal made the surprise announcement in his post-match news conference, stating he plans to never return to the club he previously served as a player and assistant coach.

He came back to Fenerbahce for a fourth spell as manager in June 2026, with the club returning to the Champions League for the first time in 18 years.

Now he departs with the team sitting ninth in the Turkish Super Lig after two wins and two defeats, and after only one Champions League match.

"I have been here three months. From the beginning of the season until today, the training sessions and camps we held with the players, and the efforts of our president, have been very helpful. Those were wonderful days," Kartal said.

"As of this evening, I congratulate my players and resign from my position.

"I made this decision to pave the way for my club. We made this decision together as a team.

"From now on, to help Fenerbahce, my players and future coaches, I have resigned from my position, with the intention of never returning."

Club president Aziz Yildirim has not accepted 65-year-old Kartal's resignation.

Yildirim said in a statement released on Fenerbahce's website, external: "Ismail Kartal is still in charge. The club should support our coach. Until I leave, Ismail Kartal is the head coach of Fenerbahce."

Yildirim confirmed he spoke to Kartal following the news conference, with the coach citing "pressure" of the role and a mid-match incident where he was struck by a bottle thrown from the stands as factors in his decision.

In a post on social media, the club said a spectator involved in the bottle incident has been identified and banned from the stadium.

Yildirim criticised the attitude of the club's supporters and the media, pinpointing the "pressure" created by the constant criticism and calling for both parties to "uphold the values of the Fenerbahce community" and show greater respect to Kartal.

Doubling down on Kartal's future, he said: "This community should support Ismail Kartal. You can't show support by throwing punches at him like this.

"Ismail Kartal doesn't need to say he'll continue. I am his senior. I said he'll continue, and that's it. We're a family."

Kartal's announcement came as a shock to Fenerbahce's players, with English defender Archie Brown, whose 48th-minute equaliser cancelled out Bryan Cristante's first-half effort for Italian side Roma, completely taken aback in a post-match interview.

When informed of Kartal's resignation, Brown said: "What do you mean he resigned? As coach? He's not the coach any more? He said this just now? I didn't know about this."

Kartal won the Turkish Super Cup in 2014 during his first spell as manager, having previously spent four years as an assistant coach. As a player, he won two league titles among six trophies with the club.

title: England captain Jones calls for fertility support
description: England captain Meg Jones wants the Red Roses to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.
fullText:
Meg Jones, captain of the England women's rugby union team, wants Red Roses players to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Jones said: "Why should my opportunity to have a family be taken away from me because I want to pursue my career?"

Jones revealed she has already started her fertility journey with her fiancee after visiting a clinic to have their egg count checked.

The 29-year-old says that she's an "open book" on some subjects and wants to "share her journey" as she discusses both her upcoming wedding and family planning with equal comfort.

"We were looking to freeze, but actually the advice was we don't need to freeze yet so we can probably wait till after the wedding," said Jones. "That's where we were going to look to conceive."

The Red Roses are considered to have one of the best maternity policies in international women's sport, with two World Cup winners having recently given birth and two more expecting.

When approached about providing fertility packages for England players, a Rugby Football Union (RFU) spokesperson said: "We work hard to support players in the decisions they make around fertility and family planning and are proud to have been at the forefront of industry-leading support in this area.

"We already have comprehensive maternity and parental policies in place and are always open to exploring how that support can evolve."

While there is no specific policy around financial compensation for fertility treatment for England players, it is understood there are ongoing discussions at the RFU and it could be introduced in the future.

Players are currently entitled to a week of paid leave per treatment cycle for treatment and appointments.

Jones first said that the Red Roses should "jump on that" policy while on the "The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby" podcast when discussing the Spanish football federation's announcement, external that it would pay for its international women's players to freeze their eggs

In August, Chelsea women also unveiled a partnership, external with a fertility company to provide workshops, treatments, counselling and assessments to support their players.

It was revealed in The Observer, external that the fund set up by Chelsea would cover the cost of the whole squad freezing their eggs.

Speaking before England's match with Australia on Saturday, Jones told BBC Sport: "I wouldn't have thought it was something that we were lacking from maybe a governing point of view, but now I think about it I'm like, yeah, actually, I haven't got that opportunity to go and create a family and be guided on.

"It's definitely been flagged with our group. Again, you learn so much from other teams… and I think the more we can empower women the better for the game as a whole, and better for women in general."

title: Two goals in two games - Sesko gives Man Utd a different threat
description: Benjamin Sesko's return to Manchester United's starting line-up is well timed ahead of Sunday's Premier League encounter with Manchester City
fullText:
Manchester United will experience far stiffer tests of their Champions League credentials than Sabah FK gave them at Old Trafford.

In fact, it would be no surprise if the Azerbaijani champions were by some distance the weakest of the eight league stage opponents Michael Carrick's side will come up against.

However, there were some important lessons for head coach Carrick to absorb.

The biggest of them is that United are a much more effective unit when Benjamin Sesko starts.

This was the first time the Slovenian had done that since the Liverpool game last March, when he finally accepted he could no longer play through the shin issue that had been plaguing him for a number of weeks.

It had been hoped Sesko would be fit for the start of the Premier League season.

As it turned out, he was only at the stage where he could be brought on as a substitute in the second half of the opening-day trip to Hull. The same also applied for the subsequent outings against Ipswich and Everton.

It was Sabah's bad luck that Sesko was fit to start against them – and it showed.

At 6ft 5in, the 23-year-old has a physical presence United's other strikers lack.

Amad Diallo's current absence has robbed Carrick of the option to start Bryan Mbeumo at the head of his attack, as he did during pre-season, but Matheus Cunha is not without ability in that role.

The problem is that the Brazilian likes to drift and drop back into space, which leaves a gap at the apex of Manchester United's attack.

Sesko offers a totally different threat. He pushes defences back. He is not easy to dispossess. He runs at opponents rather than away from them.

At Everton, it was his size that allowed him to convert a close-range header that looked set to give United victory but ultimately didn't, because of Ainsley Maitland-Niles' stunning late strike.

Against Sabah FK, Sesko had threatened with an impudent first-half back-flick before Mbeumo sent him running beyond the visitors' defence.

Sesko had clarity of thought, swiftly moving the ball past goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov before steering the ball into an empty net.

"Of course, I'm happy with my goal," Sesko told TNT after the game.

"I saw him rushing out, and it was a great opportunity to take the ball away from him and make the goal a little bit easier."

United's scenario is not that Mbeumo and Cunha can't do that, it is more that Sesko can do it in addition to presenting the physical threat.

'Good control for a big man' is one of football's oldest cliches. Yet the players who can combine size with skill and pace are exceptionally useful.

"He definitely offers a different kind of threat," said Carrick.

"That's the beauty of it, really. We know what Ben gives us. There's not many around that kind of give you what Ben does in terms of his physique, his physicality, playing on the last line and his speed to run in behind. He's a real threat.

"It's great to have him back at this level after working to get his fitness back.

"A couple of goals and good performances, and good minutes in him. I'm really pleased with the way he's gone."

It is a fairly obvious thing to say but Carrick now has a big decision before Sunday's Premier League derby with Manchester City at Old Trafford.

Does he trust Sesko's fitness and stick with him? Or does he revert to Cunha, given there has been no indication Amad is ready to return.

On this evidence, Sesko should get the nod. That in turn would leave Carrick to decide whether Cunha, who opened the scoring against Sabah, or Marcus Rashford, who was an unused substitute, should start on the left.

Rashford has yet to score a goal or create one since he returned to his boyhood club after last season's loan spell at Barcelona.

However, he has been their most consistent threat with his pace and direct running.

Cunha drifts into similar positions to skipper Bruno Fernandes, and Carrick may decide United's structure works better with England international Rashford.

If that is the case, he wasn't admitting it on a night when Fernandes also scored.

"It's not an easy decision, of course it's not," Carrick said of his team selection.

"But it's definitely one I'd prefer: to have goals in the team and for the boys to be playing well.

"The understanding they all have is that sometimes it's going to be a start, sometimes it's going to be finishing the game. We need that within the group, from game to game over the season, to be able to call upon slightly different kind of things at different times.

"It's fantastic they're all in good form and started so well."

title: 2030 Winter Olympics boss departs amid turmoil
description: Edgar Grospiron leaves his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
fullText:
Edgar Grospiron has left his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.

The departure of Grospiron, the 1992 Olympic moguls champion, was confirmed at a meeting of the committee's executive board on Thursday, marking the latest setback in the event's troubled governance.

In a statement, the organising committee said: "His decision to leave the presidency is part of a deliberate, organised and fully assumed transition, taken in the interests of the project and its governance.

"It reflects a shared desire with stakeholders to enable the organisation to quickly enter this new operational phase."

Confirming his departure via a post on LinkedIn, Grospiron said his decision followed "months of tension".

"I draw the conclusion that the conditions are not met for me to continue this," he wrote.

Grospiron's tenure, which began in February 2025, has been plagued by internal turmoil and logistical challenges.

In February 2026, chief executive officer Cyril Linette left the committee, citing "insurmountable disagreements" with Grospiron.

Linette's departure followed a number of other high-profile resignations, including chief operating officer Anne Murac and communications director Arthur Richer.

Budget cuts have plagued the planning process, with Grospiron admitting in February they had "little time, little money".

However, he remained confident he could "deliver a Games that will honour our vision and ambition" provided there was "serenity" and "continuity" from the organising committee.

In May, the committee was forced to shelve the Games' 'ice sports hub' in Nice after the city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow OGC Nice's Allianz Riviera Stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.

The ice events will now be hosted in Lyon, with the exception of speed skating, which will take place in Heerenveen in the Netherlands.

Two months later, following a tense board meeting in July, French Olympic Committee president Amelie Oudea-Castera told La Tribune Dimanche, external that they were "once again facing governance problems".

Despite another departure from the organising committee, French sports minister Marina Ferrari says there is "no concern about what comes next".

"The bid is continuing to move forward," she told reporters. "Our teams are mobilised and working. We are confident about the future of the Alpes project."

The International Olympic Committee praised Grospiron's "crucial work in laying the foundations for the success" of the Games.

"The IOC will continue working in close collaboration with the organising committee to build on the solid foundations that Mr Grospiron has laid," the statement added.

fullText:
Report comes two days after former employee quit claiming company’s models could cause human extinction by 2030

Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday.

“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.”

In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work.

“Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.”

Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent.

Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions.

In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms.

Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute.

The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him.

Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence.

“AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly.

In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations.

The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses.

“As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.
